extracted.intended_audience: research funders, policy-makers, programme managers, and researchers involved in grant peer review and research funding allocation
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesis and assessment of evidence about how well grant peer review in the health sciences performs (effectiveness, reliability, fairness, timeliness, burden) and what design features/interventions affect those outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of peer review in awarding grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Does peer review fund the 'best' science? (Includes claims that peer review may not fund the most innovative, interdisciplinary or applied research, and may only weakly predict future research performance.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarises Table 3: major critiques are anti-innovation (Yes; suggestive evidence), weak predictor of future performance (Yes; agreement), unreliability (ratings vary considerably between reviewers; yes), unfairness (gender/age/cognitive particularism/cronyism: mixed/conflicting evidence). Use empirical studies (bibliometric comparisons, outcome tracking) to judge predictive validity; acknowledge that 'best' science is not fixed and may include innovation, interdisciplinarity and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (bias against innovative/high-risk research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review disfavors innovative or high-risk proposals because they lack preceding work and require less risk-averse reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence suggests innovative proposals score lower even after controlling for feasibility. Approaches include: recruit reviewers who value high-risk research, explicitly include 'innovation' as an assessment criterion, increase weight given to innovation, use disagreement among reviewers as a signal of innovation, or fund researchers (not specified projects). Delphi processes and dedicated high-risk schemes (e.g., NIH Pioneer) are possible mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair assessment of interdisciplinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review fairly evaluates interdisciplinary proposals given difficulties locating peers and combining distinct quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (e.g., Australian Research Council data) shows increased interdisciplinarity associated with lower success. Remedies suggested: larger panels with broader expertise (at cost of burden), change role of in-depth reviewers, broaden panel composition carefully. Be aware that mixing disciplines often reduces inter-rater agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair assessment of applied/translational research
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review disadvantages applied or translational research (e.g., because of emphasis on scholarly tests over impact and different publication patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooksey and other reports note peer review can inhibit applied work. Mitigations: include research users on panels, assess likely impact at application stage, use 'merit review' panels combining academic and user/policy perspectives. Evidence base is limited and mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity (peer review as predictor of future performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which grant peer review scores/rankings predict subsequent research performance (e.g., bibliometrics, commercial success).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple studies find little or weak association between application rankings and later bibliometric outcomes; some evidence reviewers can reliably identify the top ~20–30% but not reliably the top 10%. Use multiple outcome measures cautiously; bibliometrics are imperfect proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability / inter-rater agreement / decision consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: How consistent are reviewers' ratings of the same proposal and how consistent are panel/funder decisions (single-rater reliabilities, intra-class correlations, panel agreement rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported single-rater correlations often low (~0.19–0.23); panel agreement studies show mixed results (e.g., 65–83% agreement). Panel discussion often changes decisions for only ~10% of applications. Options to improve: reviewer training (see NIH elements), evaluating review quality, use mean reviewer scores instead of relying on meeting re-rating, and experiment with virtual panels. Expect variability by field and panel composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias — gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review outcomes are affected by applicant gender (claims of sexism/nepotism vs studies finding no systematic bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is conflicting: some large-scale studies and meta-analyses show small male advantage, others find no bias. Interpret results cautiously, consider study designs (blinded vs unblinded) and wider systemic effects (pipeline and career-stage differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias — age / early-career disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential bias in peer review against older or early-career researchers due to use of past publications/funding or age effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence is mixed/conflicting: some studies find declines in success with age, others find no direct effect. Funders (e.g., NIH) have adopted measures to equalise success for new investigators. Consider eligibility/award criteria that may implicitly disadvantage career stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism / conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which applicants' prior affiliations or relationships with reviewers/panelists increase success (nepotism/cronyism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies indicate prior affiliation can increase chances of funding. Funders typically have conflict-of-interest procedures; anonymisation and strict COI rules help but may exclude the best experts. Be mindful that panel membership correlates with higher submission and award rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism (disciplinary/self‑interest bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency for reviewers to favour proposals in their own field or aligned with their way of thinking (or conversely to be more critical of work in their expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence mixed: some studies show favouring own fields; others show higher criticism of closely familiar work. 'Cognitive distance' can produce non-linear effects. Possible remedies: include senior generalists, broaden the range of fields judged by each group, but balance against loss of expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: How long the peer review process takes from submission to funding decision and whether delays harm research (e.g., during epidemics or for time-sensitive projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process can take 9–18 months. Longer times may hinder research progress or economic viability. Consider streamlining, triage, accelerated review tracks, or alternative allocation mechanisms for urgent or time-critical funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and efficiency (time/cost of peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The workload and resources consumed by peer review for applicants, reviewers, and funders; who bears the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good evidence that burden is high and ~75% falls on applicants. Many reduction efforts target funders/reviewers, not applicants. Consider shorter proposals, triage, virtual meetings, reduced application formats, or alternative allocation mechanisms to reduce applicant burden. Account for hidden systemic costs when designing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness of review processes, clarity of decision rationale, and mechanisms for stakeholders to assess performance and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity can reduce transparency. Authors recommend funders acknowledge and analyse uncertainty (e.g., capture reviewers' uncertainty), open data on review scores, experiment transparently, and use openness to evaluate alternative allocation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymisation / blinding of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of blinded (anonymised) proposals to reduce bias based on applicant identity, institution, gender, or race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding provides some defence against identity-based bias but may be imperfect (identification possible from content) and evidence is mixed. Short anonymised versions sometimes correlate weakly with full unblinded reviews; disentangle length/content effects from blinding effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: How the disciplinary, professional (research/practice/policy), and demographic makeup of panels affects review outcomes, reliability and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity can reduce inter-rater reliability (different backgrounds yield lower agreement) and affect outcomes (e.g., favoring certain approaches). Remedies include careful balancing of expertise, larger panels for interdisciplinarity, and awareness of trade-offs between expertise and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of panel meetings and deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of panel discussion/meetings (face-to-face, teleconference, virtual) on final scores and funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report limited net effect of meetings on changing final outcomes (often ~10% of applications affected). Some funders find mean reviewer scores approximate panel consensus, suggesting triage or relying on averages may be practical and economical. Virtual panels produce similar scoring but participants value face-to-face social aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training (NIH recommended elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training topics suggested to improve reviewer behaviour and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH recommended training to: (1) emphasise strengths rather than rewrite proposals, (2) focus on potential impact, (3) review the merit not re-write, (4) recognise implicit bias, (5) use benchmark applications during panel meetings, and (6) note potential bias towards lesser-known organisations. Brief training has been shown in one study to increase inter-rater reliability substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of review quality (meta-review of reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing and rating the quality of the reviews themselves using criteria such as completeness and usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European Science Foundation survey reports funders evaluate reviews on completeness, level of substantiation, appropriateness, comprehensibility, timeliness and usefulness; poor reviews may be returned or rejected. Adding this step increases burden but may improve review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using score distributions and reviewer disagreement as signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting high disagreement among reviewers as a potential indicator of innovative/high-risk proposals or of evaluative uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some analyses suggest high disagreement could identify novel proposals worth consideration. Funders might explicitly use variance/dispersion of scores as an input (not just mean), or weight criteria typically underweighted by reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random allocation / lottery as an allocation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a lottery element in funding decisions (e.g., among near-equal proposals) to reduce burden and bias and enable evaluation of processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest funders could consider lotteries in some parts of allocation to reduce burden and bias, and to allow better evaluation of decision processes. This is proposed as an alternative to purely rank-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of evidence quality for studies on peer review (GRADE-style scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework used in the review to rate quality/strength of evidence for each area of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box 1 scale: 1 Assumptions (intuitive beliefs), 2 Suggestive (insufficient but suggestive), 3 Conflicting (conflicting results from well-conducted studies), 4 Agreement (several well-conducted studies agree), 5 Compelling (systematic reviews are compelling). Use this to aggregate strength of evidence when synthesising findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection on investigator (track record) vs selection on project
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to fund researchers based on prior merit/person rather than specific proposed projects (e.g., fellowships like MacArthur Fellows) as an alternative allocation principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach may allow researchers freedom to pursue novel ideas without conservative project-based review. It sidesteps project-level bias but changes incentives and assessment criteria; consider suitability for programme aims.
